result.content:
# Shot listing

Breaking a scene into shots. Read `scene-context.md` first — the six department
answers are what fill each shot's atmosphere.

Before starting, read the scene node, the characters in it from the bible, the
location, and any set design or wardrobe attached to the scene. If the location
has generated views, look at which angles exist. Composing shots for a space you
can see produces better coverage than composing for a slugline, which is why
building the set first is usually worth it — though a director who already knows
the room can skip it.

---

## Build atmosphere before faces

**Shot 1 is the space, not a person.** A wide or establishing frame showing the
full location, with characters absent or as small silhouettes. The audience
needs to know where they are before they are asked to care what happens there.

**Shot 2 is usually a detail.** A texture, an object, an atmospheric element.
This is what gives a scene weight rather than urgency.

Faces and dialogue start from shot 3. Cutting to a close-up in the first frame
of a scene is a music-video instinct; it burns the location and leaves the
audience spatially lost.

Think Fincher or Villeneuve rather than a trailer. Do not rush.

## Every cut needs a shot

This is a shot division, not a storyboard. You are not selecting the memorable
moments — you are providing a frame for every edit point.

Between any two significant actions there is: the action, the reaction, an
insert of whatever object is involved, and the transitional beat that gets from
one to the other. If a character crosses a room, that is the start, the
crossing, and the arrival — not just the arrival.

Sit at the timeline. Every three to ten seconds is a new shot. A scene that
should run 45 seconds and produces four shots has skipped the connective tissue,
and it will cut like a slideshow.

## Objects get their own frame

If the screenplay names an object — a cigarette, a phone, a glass, a weapon —
give it an extreme close-up before or during the interaction with it.

The insert is how an object becomes significant. A gun that only appears in wide
shots is set dressing. A gun that gets a macro on the trigger guard is a threat.

## Eye-lines and the 180-degree rule

When two characters interact, know where each is looking. Cross the line and the
audience loses which way people face; the scene stops being a conversation and
becomes two monologues.

State positions explicitly — who is standing, who is sitting, what furniture
they are near. Without this, consecutive shots will place the same character in
physically impossible relationships to the room.

## Lens variety

Use real terminology, because it carries framing, compression, and distance in
one phrase: *Tight 85mm on eyes*, *Low-angle wide 24mm*, *Macro 100mm*,
*Over-the-shoulder*, *Medium 50mm*.

Vary it. Ten shots at the same focal length is not coverage, it is repetition.
Wide for geography, medium for relationship, long lens for isolation and
compression, macro for significance.

## Beats, not just lines

The interesting frame is often not the line — it is the micro-expression before
it, or the reaction three seconds after. A shot list built only around dialogue
misses where the scene actually turns.

## Coverage follows subtext

When two shots are both technically correct, choose the one that serves the
power dynamic. Tightening on someone losing control, staying on the listener
during a lie, giving air to whoever holds the room. This is the difference
between covering a scene and directing it.

---

## What each shot needs

- **`visual_action`** — what the camera sees, written as a cinematographer's
  description. This is the text the image is generated from, so it is the most
  important field on the shot. Describe the frame: subject, position, what is
  behind them, the quality of light, the texture. Name characters by name and
  describe their appearance from their bible traits. Everything below supports
  this field; none of it replaces it.
- **`shot_type`** — the lens and framing, in professional terms.
- **`camera_direction`** — where the camera physically is and what it faces.
  "Camera low near the centre of the room, looking toward the far doors."
- **`ambient_scene`** — the environmental state: light quality, atmosphere,
  mood. This comes straight from the six department answers. If it reads
  generically, the department pass was skipped.
- **`continuity_note`** — how this shot connects to the previous one, and where
  everyone and everything is standing. Both halves matter; the edit connection
  without the positions is not enough to keep the space coherent.
- **`characters`** — only who is visible in this frame. An ECU holds one person.
  An over-the-shoulder holds two. A wide may hold none.
- **`products`** — only what is actually in this frame, not everything in the
  scene.
- **`estimated_duration`** — how long this take runs. The shot durations should
  sum to roughly the scene's estimated duration; if they don't, either the
  coverage or the estimate is wrong.

Each shot is one continuous take from one camera position. If a shot needs the
camera to be in two places, or contains more than a couple of distinct actions,
it is two shots.

## Location angles

If the location has generated views, each shot should name which one it is
shooting against — the wall or background visible behind the subject. Choose
from what actually exists; a shot composed against a wall with no reference will
be generated blind and will not match the rest of the scene.

Vary the angles. A scene shot entirely against one wall feels like a stage set.
Three or more different backgrounds across a scene of any length reads as a real
room.

## Stay inside the screenplay

Every shot maps to a beat, action line, or dialogue exchange that is actually in
the scene. Do not invent dialogue and do not invent action. Coverage is a
reading of the scene, not an extension of it.

---

## Reviewing your own list

Before finishing, read the list back as an edit and cut what fails:

- **Redundant** — two shots at similar angle and content. Keep the stronger.
- **Spatially impossible** — a position that contradicts an earlier shot or the
  set layout.
- **Low value** — a shot that neither advances the scene nor builds atmosphere.
- **Underspecified** — generic lighting or atmosphere, a character with no
  wardrobe, a frame that could belong to any scene in any film. Fix rather than
  cut: the department answers already hold what is missing.

Then check the whole against the scene: does the light match the `time` field
throughout, does the grade match the moodboard, does every named character
resolve to someone in the bible.

node.synopsis: The room is suffocatingly silent. The Man sits on the edge of The Bed, fully visible now, wearing standard men's clothing. Scattered on the floor nearby lie the Evening Heels and the Handbag. He slowly raises his head, looking directly into the Large Bedroom Mirror across the room. The reflection is just him, stark and unglamorous. Trembling slightly, he reaches out and picks up the Lipstick left on the vanity. result.content:
# Scene context

Read this before breaking a scene into shots, or when a scene's shots feel
generic — technically correct framing that could belong to any film.

A scene is not just an action line. Before covering it, a real production has
six people looking at the same page and seeing different things. Work through
all six yourself. It takes one pass and it is the difference between "medium
shot of two people talking" and a shot that carries the scene.

Do not treat these as six separate jobs to hand off. It is one reading from six
angles, and the value is in how they contradict each other — the gaffer wants
the practical lamp motivated, the colorist wants the shadows crushed, and
resolving that tension is the actual decision.

---

## Gaffer — light

What is the key, where is it coming from, and is it motivated by something in
frame? Practicals matter: a streetlamp, a laptop, a match. If the light has no
source in the world, the image reads as rendered rather than photographed.

Ask what shifts during the scene. Light that changes — a door opening, a car
passing, a cigarette flaring — gives an editor something to cut on and gives the
scene a clock.

Check the scene's `time` field and let it govern everything here. A night
interior lit like golden hour is the single most common failure, and it survives
because every individual shot prompt reads plausibly on its own.

## VFX — air

Not explosions. The small environmental things that make a frame feel inhabited:
dust in a shaft of light, breath in cold air, steam, rain on glass, heat
shimmer, smoke, lens flare from a practical.

A room with clean empty air looks like a render. One atmospheric element per
shot is usually enough, and it should be consistent across the scene — dust
motes in shot 2 and pristine air in shot 5 is a continuity break nobody can
name but everybody feels.

## Hair & makeup — state

Not what a character looks like in general — the bible already holds that. What
they look like *now*, in this scene, after what has just happened to them.

Sweating, crying, bleeding, immaculate, disheveled, drunk, exhausted, freshly
showered. This is where a scene's place in the story becomes visible on a face.
If a character was running in the previous scene and arrives composed in this
one, the cut will read as a mistake.

## Key grip — camera energy

Locked-off, handheld, or smooth? This is a decision about control.

Static framing gives the audience nowhere to look away — it suits menace,
formality, and dread. Handheld puts the viewer inside a body and suits panic and
intimacy. Smooth movement suits elegance, wealth, and inevitability.

Pick one energy for the scene and hold it. Mixing them without reason makes the
coverage feel assembled rather than directed.

## Colorist — grade

The project moodboard sets the palette. Ask what this specific scene does within
it: is it the warmest scene in a cold film, the one moment of saturation, the
point where the grade starts to drain?

A grade that never varies across a film is a look. A grade that shifts with the
story is cinematography.

**The moodboard is a grade and an atmosphere, not a set dressing list.** If the
moodboard says "neon reflections, wet asphalt," that does not mean every scene
gains neon signs and rain. It means the colour separation and the quality of
light. Applying moodboard keywords as objects is the most common way a scene
ends up with props nobody asked for.

## Subtext — what is unsaid

What is actually happening under the dialogue? Who has power at the start of the
scene, who has it at the end, and where does it change hands?

This is what tells you where to put the camera. If a character is losing
control, the coverage can tighten on them while their opposite is given air. If
someone is lying, the camera can stay on the listener. Subtext is the reason to
prefer one shot over another when both are technically fine.

---

## Using this

Write the six down before listing shots. Keep them short — a line or two each.
They are working notes, not a document.

Then, when you write each shot, the light, the air, the state, the energy, and
the grade all have answers already. That is what `ambient_scene` is for, and why
a shot that skips this reads as a description of an event rather than a frame.

If the scene has set design, wardrobe, or a location with spatial notes, read
those first — they constrain the gaffer and the colorist answers, and it is
cheaper to read them than to write a shot list that contradicts the set.

node.spatial_context:
**LEFT PERIMETER**
A dark teal wall featuring intricate gold rectangular paneling. It grounds a massive, king-sized bed with a deep navy velvet, diamond-tufted headboard. The bed is a chaotic mound of heavy silk and velvet linens in deep blues and silvers. 

**RIGHT PERIMETER**
A heavily textured dark teal wall dominated by a colossal, floor-to-ceiling antique mirror. The mirror features a highly ornate, thick gold-leaf frame and reflects the bed, scattered garments, and the opposing gold-trimmed wall. 

**SKY**
An off-white, smooth ceiling bordered by deep, multi-tiered classical crown molding. It is illuminated by a soft, warm, diffuse overhead light, creating a glowing amber gradient that fades toward the room's corners. 

**GROUND**
Wide-plank, distressed dark mahogany hardwood flooring with a slight reflective sheen. The floor is heavily shadowed and littered with discarded luxury items: a black leather jacket, crumpled silk dresses, scattered stilettos, and leather handbags. 

**FAR END**
Two tall, dark-framed windows obscured by heavy, floor-to-ceiling brown velvet drapes. To the right, imposing double doors—dark wood with elaborate gold filigree panels—stand ajar. They spill a sharp, intense, golden-hour light from an adjacent hallway into the moody bedroom, creating long shadows.

**NEAR END**
A grand, black marble fireplace mantel flanked by the same gold-trimmed teal wainscoting seen throughout the room. Above the mantel hangs an imposing, dark oil painting. To the sides of the hearth sit two deep, tufted navy leather wingback chairs. The glowing embers in the hearth cast a faint, flickering amber under-light, providing the warm specular highlights seen on the leather jacket tossed on the floor.

model.text:
I've broken Scene 2 down into a 7-shot sequence that honors the heavy, silent atmosphere of the room and the emotional weight of the scene. The visual direction leans into the project's chiaroscuro look, utilizing the midnight cyan shadows, rich antique golds, and soft amber lighting from the hallway and fireplace.

Here is a summary of the shot list built for this scene:

*   **Shot 1 (Wide 24mm):** The establishing space. We see the heavy, suffocating mood of the room. The scattered Evening Heels and Handbag rest in the foreground, with the Man sitting small and isolated on The Bed in the midground, contrasting against a warm spill of light from the ajar hallway doors.
*   **Shot 2 (Medium Wide 50mm):** The detail/texture. We look at the Large Bedroom Mirror and its ornate gold-leaf filigree reflecting the still, defeated posture of the Man sitting on the bed. 
*   **Shot 3 (Medium Close-Up 85mm):** The first movement. From an angle pointing at the dark teal wall, we see the Man raise his head to look off-camera, his rigid, guarded posture caught in a soft frontal-left key light.
*   **Shot 4 (Close-Up 100mm):** The eye-line and reaction. An over-the-shoulder look directly into the Large Bedroom Mirror, capturing his stark reflection and the trembling denial in his jaw against an obsidian background.
*   **Shot 5 (Macro Insert 100mm):** Object significance. A very tight insert of his trembling hand reaching into the vanity area to pick up the heavy, chipped-gold Lipstick.
*   **Shot 6 (Medium Close-Up 50mm, High Angle):** Action and inspection. The camera looks slightly down as he turns the metallic tube over in his hands, highlighting the peachy skin and warm glow against the oppressive dark voids of the room.
*   **Shot 7 (Tight 85mm):** The climax of the beat. A slight tracking push-in as he brings both hands up, burying his face in his hands (gripping the lipstick), disappearing into the deep shadows.

All seven shots have been written to `/Not Yet/sc2/sh1` through `/Not Yet/sc2/sh7` in the project tree.
